reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Defined by the triad of micrognathia, glossoptosis (posterior tongue displacement), and consequent upper airway obstruction, frequently with a U-shaped cleft palate
It is a sequence rather than a syndrome, meaning one initiating event (mandibular hypoplasia) cascades into the other features
Airway obstruction is often positional and may improve with prone or lateral positioning in milder cases
Feeding difficulty is common and closely linked to the degree of airway compromise
It may be isolated or part of a broader syndrome, most commonly Stickler syndrome, so systemic and ophthalmological review is important
Mandibular catch-up growth over the first years often improves airway and feeding without major surgery in milder cases
Severity ranges from mild positional obstruction to critical airway compromise requiring surgical intervention
reference.pathophysiology: The sequence is initiated by early hypoplasia of the mandible. The small jaw leaves insufficient room in the oral cavity, so the tongue is displaced posteriorly and superiorly (glossoptosis), which in turn obstructs the airway and, during palatal shelf fusion, mechanically prevents the shelves meeting, producing the characteristic wide U-shaped cleft palate. The initiating mandibular deficiency may result from intrinsic developmental disturbance of the first branchial arch or from extrinsic constraint such as oligohydramnios limiting jaw movement in utero. Because a single early anomaly drives the downstream features, the condition is classified as a malformation sequence, and it may occur in isolation or as a component of a recognisable syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Neuromuscular causes of glossoptosis and hypotonia
additionalInvestigations: Sleep study or overnight oximetry to quantify obstructive events and desaturation
Flexible nasendoscopy to characterise the level and mechanism of airway obstruction
Feeding and swallowing assessment with monitoring of weight gain
Ophthalmological review and genetic evaluation to identify Stickler and other syndromes
Echocardiography where a syndromic association is suspected
Molecular or chromosomal testing guided by associated anomalies
redFlags: Severe or worsening obstructive apnoea with desaturation or cor pulmonale
Failure to thrive from inability to feed safely
Cyanotic episodes or respiratory distress unrelieved by positioning
Signs of a wider syndrome requiring urgent multisystem evaluation
reference.prognosis: Isolated Robin sequence generally has a favourable outlook as mandibular growth improves the airway over time, whereas syndromic cases and those with severe obstruction carry greater morbidity and depend on the associated condition.
pitfalls: Treating it as a fixed syndrome rather than recognising an initiating sequence
Failing to look for an underlying syndrome, especially Stickler
Underestimating airway obstruction because the infant appears settled when prone
Overlooking feeding failure as a marker of significant obstruction
Delaying escalation when non-surgical measures are insufficient
